draft.title: Lines, stanzas and free verse
card: a single row of words in a poem. The poet chooses where each line ends, so a line can stop in the middle of a sentence.
a group of lines set apart from the next group by a blank space. A stanza works a bit like a paragraph in prose, often holding one idea or moment.
a poem with no regular rhyme pattern and no steady rhythm. The poet has no set pattern to follow.
Because free verse has no pattern, line breaks and stanza breaks do more of the work. A very short line can make a word stand out, and a gap can make the reader pause.
draft.remember: Lines and stanzas shape a poem on the page. In free verse, the line breaks matter more.

a.q: Which of these is a stanza?
opts: A group of lines set apart by a blank space
A single word that is repeated in a poem
The pair of words that rhyme at the line ends
The title that is written above the poem
a.why: A stanza is a group of lines set apart from the next group by a space. A line is only one row of words, and rhyming words are about sound, not about how the poem is grouped.
a.clue: Think of how a paragraph is grouped in prose.

b.q: Zara writes a poem with no rhyme and no steady beat. She puts the word "alone" on a line by itself. What is the most likely effect?
opts: It makes the word stand out and gives the reader a pause
It gives the poem a regular rhyme pattern at the line ends
It turns the poem into a single stanza of equal lines
It shows the poem is not free verse because it has a pattern
b.why: A poem with no rhyme and no steady beat is free verse, so line breaks do more of the work. A word on its own line stands out and slows the reader. Putting one word on a line does not add rhyme or make a regular pattern.
b.clue: What does a very short line do to the one word in it?

a.best: A group of lines set apart by a blank space

b.best: It makes the word stand out and gives the reader a pause
